teaser.text: Lenovo Group Limited makes the machines people use, the systems behind them, and the services that keep both useful. Its business is easiest to understand as a chain: equipment is designed and delivered, customers pay through several routes, and Lenovo pays suppliers, workers, partners, and the cost of supporting what it sells.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Lenovo, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The base case assumes operating profit rises as infrastructure and services improve, but does not assume management achieves every ambition. The historical average was US$2,636.214 million, while FY2026 reached US$3,261.743 million. The June ISG margin of 9.1% supports upside, but it is only one quarter. The bear case reflects another PC downturn, slow AI conversion and discounting; the bull requires sustained AI-server delivery, resilient premium PCs and high SSG profitability.

The bear case requires weaker PC demand, rising inventory, delayed AI orders and lower-margin infrastructure work. Cash pressure then limits buybacks and leaves dilution exposed. It gives HKD 15.13 in October 2027 and HKD 9.93 in October 2029. Its 30% probability reflects Lenovo’s two-year operating-profit downturn and the recent working-capital surge, although profitable IDG and SSG make a prolonged collapse less likely.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Lenovo really make?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is operating cash after capital spending and lease payments. Deducting stock-based pay gives a stricter economic measure because employees receive value that shareholders ultimately fund through dilution or repurchases. The cash-conversion cycle measures the time between paying for inputs and collecting customer cash, so rising inventory or slower customers can weaken it.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Lenovo today?

paragraphs.text: The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, shows how much investors pay for one dollar of annual profit. Lenovo’s trailing P/E is 63.9x, while its next-twelve-month P/E is 15.1x. The gap exists because June 2026 accounts recorded a US$1,690 million warrant revaluation loss and a US$609 million reported shareholder loss. Adjusted shareholder profit was US$1,075 million.

blocks.heading: Does Lenovo's cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left after operating needs and investment in the business have been paid for. Across the five years ended March 2022–2026, Lenovo generated US$6,181.852 million of free cash flow and paid US$4,741.112 million to shareholders before payments to minority owners. The pattern was uneven: payments continued when free cash flow was negative or unusually weak. That means some distributions came from cash already held, borrowing or working-capital changes.

paragraphs.text: The decision points are whether ISG sustains profit as it grows, whether inventory and collections improve, and whether late-2026 Riyadh production moves from a first product to reliable customer shipments. Memory pressure is expected through the end of 2027. November 19, 2026 interim results will test profit, cash, inventory and collections. January 2028 brings the Alat bond decision: conversion reduces repayment needs but raises the share count.

blocks.heading: What has Lenovo guided for the year ending March 2027?

paragraphs.text: Management first set the revenue goal alongside its May 2026 results. By August, chairman and chief executive Yang Yuanqing said the first-quarter momentum made the target achievable in the financial year ending March 2027. That is an acceleration of the timetable, not a detailed quarterly forecast.

The profitability goal runs on a different clock. Lenovo is working toward a net income margin above 5%, meaning the share of sales left for shareholders after expenses, financing costs and tax. At the intended scale, a five-per-cent margin would leave $5 billion in annual profit. The revenue and margin goals should therefore not be treated as a promise to arrive together.

blocks.heading: Did Lenovo keep its past promise?

paragraphs.text: Lenovo also promised to double net margin by the end of FY2023/24. Net margin means net income kept from each dollar of revenue. The starting year produced about US$1.2 billion of net income on US$60.7 billion of revenue. FY2023/24 produced about US$1 billion on US$56.9 billion of revenue, leaving margins of roughly 2.0% and 1.8%. The promised result would have been about 4.0%, so Lenovo did not deliver it.

blocks.heading: What is Lenovo's revenue and profit trend?

paragraphs.text: Cash provides the necessary check. Operating cash weakened, and free cash flow turned negative after capital spending and leases. At the same time, ISG reported a 9.1% operating margin, a striking improvement from its annual result. The quarter may mark a genuine operating turn, but the specialist needs to see that margin persist while customers pay and inventory converts.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in Lenovo's next results?

paragraphs.text: The first checkpoint is November 19, 2026, when Lenovo’s board is due to consider results for the six months ended September 30 and an interim dividend. Investors should compare revenue and adjusted profit with cash collection, inventories and supplier obligations. The dividend will also show how management balances shareholder payments against expansion.
